working: Parallel requires alpha:beta:gamma = 1:1:1, i.e. alpha=beta=gamma=k; non-coincident requires k/1 != 3/7. (A) k=1 gives x+y+z=3, parallel and distinct from x+y+z=7. (B) k=3/7 reduces to x+y+z=7 which is COINCIDENT, so it fails 'not coincident'. (C) alpha=beta=gamma alone permits k=3/7, so it does not guarantee non-coincidence.
notes: Stem is OCR-corrupted: 'alpha x + beta y + gamma z = = \ mma\ of\ the\ following\ conditions\ will\ be\ two\ planes\ 3,' — a duplicated fragment of the question text has been spliced in and the RHS constant 3 pushed to the end. Reconstructed as 'alpha x + beta y + gamma z = 3', which is the standard form of this question and is the only reading under which the options are meaningful. working: Line direction d=(2,3,4). Line parallel to plane iff d.n=0. (A) (4,3,-5): 8+9-20=-3. (B) (4,5,-4): 8+15-16=7. (C) (4,4,-5): 8+12-20=0 (ok). (D) (5,4,-5): 10+12-20=2. Also point (3,4,5) in (C): 12+16-25=3 != 0, so the line lies outside the plane and is genuinely parallel, not contained.
Take the cube [0,1]^3. Two space diagonals have direction ratios (1,1,1) and (-1,1,1). cos(theta) = |-1+1+1|/(sqrt3*sqrt3) = 1/3, so theta = arccos(1/3) = 70.53 degrees > 60 degrees.
notes: 'Diagonals of a cube' is taken in its standard sense of the four space (main) diagonals, giving arccos(1/3). If a reader instead took FACE diagonals meeting at a vertex the angle would be exactly 60 degrees and option (B) would be picked — worth knowing this is the classic distractor, but the space-diagonal reading is the intended one.

working: A plane contains the Z-axis iff every point (0,0,t) satisfies it. (A) 0-t=-t, (B) t+0=t, (D) 0+2t=2t all fail for t != 0; (C) 3(0)+2(0)=0 holds for all t. Equivalently, a plane through the Z-axis has no z-term and no constant term.
x^2+y^2-6x+2y=0 has centre (3,-1). Any diameter passes through the centre. (A) x+3y = 3+3(-1) = 0 (ok). (B) 3-1=2, (C) 3 != -1, (D) 9-1=8 all fail.
subtopic: Circle Equation — Centre, Radius, Diameter, and Properties

working: For the ellipse x^2/(a^2+lambda) + y^2/(b^2+lambda) = 1 (a>b), e^2 = 1 - (b^2+lambda)/(a^2+lambda). Let f(lambda) = (b^2+lambda)/(a^2+lambda); f'(lambda) = (a^2-b^2)/(a^2+lambda)^2 > 0, so f increases toward 1 and e^2 = 1-f strictly decreases. Hence eccentricity decreases as lambda increases.
subtopic: Ellipse — Foci, Eccentricity, and Focal Distances
notes: OCR artifact: the numerator is printed 'y\hat{}2' for y^2. The conclusion is symmetric in a,b — if b>a the major axis is vertical, e^2 = 1-(a^2+lambda)/(b^2+lambda), and the eccentricity again decreases — so (B) holds regardless of which of a,b is larger.

working: S(x,y)=x^2+y^2+4x-2y-4; S(1,2)=1+4+4-4-4=1>0, so the point is exterior. Check: centre (-2,1), radius sqrt(4+1+4)=3, distance = sqrt(9+1)=sqrt10 = 3.162 > 3.

working: Centre (-g,-f), radius sqrt(g^2+f^2-c). Touching the Y-axis (x=0) means distance from centre to that axis equals the radius: |g| = sqrt(g^2+f^2-c) => g^2 = g^2+f^2-c => f^2 = c => f = +/- sqrt(c). (Equivalently set x=0: y^2+2fy+c=0 has equal roots => f^2=c.) Since c>0 both signs are admissible, so (D) not (C).
subtopic: Circle Equation — Centre, Radius, Diameter, and Properties

working: For parallelogram ABCD the diagonals AC and BD share a midpoint. Mid AC = ((2+0)/2,(3-2)/2) = (1, 1/2). Mid BD = ((1+x)/2,(4+y)/2). So 1+x=2 => x=1 and 4+y=1 => y=-3, giving D(1,-3).
(OA)(OB)cos(angle AOB) is exactly the dot product of vectors OA=(x1,y1) and OB=(x2,y2), which equals x1x2 + y1y2.

working: dy/dx = xy+x+y+1 = x(y+1)+(y+1) = (y+1)(x+1). Separating: dy/(y+1) = (x+1)dx => log(y+1) = x^2/2 + x + c.

working: By parts with u=log(x+1), dv=dx (take v=x+1): integral = (x+1)log(x+1) - integral 1 dx = (x+1)log(x+1) - x + c. Differentiating (B): log(x+1) + 1 - 1 = log(x+1) (ok). (A) differentiates to log(x+1) + x/(x+1) - 1, which is wrong.

y = (3x-15)/5 is negative on [1,3] (y=-12/5 at x=1, y=-6/5 at x=3), so the region lies below the X-axis. Area = integral_1^3 (15-3x)/5 dx = (1/5)[15x - 3x^2/2]_1^3 = (1/5)(31.5 - 13.5) = 18/5. (Trapezium check: (1/2)(12/5+6/5)(2) = 18/5.)
subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve, Lines, and Axes

working: Highest derivative is d^2y/dx^2 => order 2. To read the degree the equation must be polynomial in the derivatives: raise both sides to the 6th power, (y'')^5 = (y')^2, so the degree (power of the highest-order derivative) is 5. Order 2, degree 5.
subtopic: Order, Degree, and Solutions of ODE

working: dx/dt = cos t - (cos t - t sin t) = t sin t; dy/dt = sin t + t cos t - sin t = t cos t. So dy/dx = cot t. At t = pi/2, cot(pi/2) = 0.
Differentiate the given identity: d/dx[log{f(x)}^2] = d/dx[2 log f(x)] = 2f'(x)/f(x), and this must equal 1/f(x). Hence 2f'(x) = 1, f'(x) = 1/2, f(x) = x/2 + alpha.
subtopic: Standard Forms — Exponential, Logarithmic, and Paired Trigonometric Integrals
notes: Read log{f(x)}^2 as log of the square, i.e. 2 log f(x) (the standard reading, and the only one that yields an option). Under the alternative reading (log f(x))^2 the equation 2 f'(x) log f(x) = 1 has no solution matching any option.

working: Perimeter 2(l+b)=200 => l+b=100. Area = l(100-l), maximised at l=50 (derivative 100-2l=0), giving 50*50 = 2500 sq m. (AM-GM: area <= ((l+b)/2)^2 = 2500, equality for the square.)
